questions.q: What is the core idea of role-based access control as described in this lesson?
options: Permissions are granted based on an employee's physical office location
Access is granted only once per calendar year regardless of role changes
Every user gets administrator access by default
Permissions attach to roles, and roles attach to people, instead of granting permissions to individuals one at a time
questions.explain: RBAC splits the problem into defining what a role needs and deciding who holds that role, so a change to the role's permissions propagates to every member automatically.

questions.q: In SQL Server, which statement is the modern way to add a user as a member of a database role?
options: UPDATE SalesAnalystRole SET member = 'jsmith';
INSERT INTO SalesAnalystRole VALUES ('jsmith');
ALTER ROLE SalesAnalystRole ADD MEMBER [DOMAIN\jsmith];
DELETE ROLE SalesAnalystRole WHERE user = 'jsmith';
questions.explain: ALTER ROLE ... ADD MEMBER is the current, non-legacy T-SQL syntax for adding a user to a database role (sp_addrolemember still works but is documented as legacy).

questions.q: If a user's role GRANTs SELECT on a table, but a separate DENY targets one column of that same table for the same role, what happens?
options: The two cancel out and the user gets REVOKE-level (undefined) access
SQL Server throws an error and refuses to apply either permission
The DENY wins — the user cannot see that column, regardless of the GRANT
The GRANT always overrides any DENY
questions.explain: DENY is an explicit block that always wins over a GRANT, even one coming from a different role the same user belongs to — this lesson's example denies SELECT on a Customers.SSN column specifically.

questions.q: What does REVOKE do, as distinct from DENY?
options: It grants a permission permanently with no way to remove it later
It is a synonym for DENY with identical behavior
It deletes the underlying table the permission was granted on
It removes a previously granted permission, returning to a neutral 'no explicit permission' state — it does not explicitly block like DENY does
questions.explain: REVOKE removes a grant and returns to neutral, while DENY actively blocks the permission and overrides any other GRANT the same user might hold.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why does RBAC make an access review (Lesson 16) faster than reviewing every user individually?
options: RBAC automatically removes stale access without any review
RBAC eliminates the need for any access reviews at all
RBAC requires every user to review their own access personally
An auditor can review a role's permission list once, then just review its membership list, instead of re-deriving each person's access from scratch
questions.explain: Because permissions live on a small number of roles rather than scattered across individual users, the review collapses to checking each role's entitlements plus its current membership.
